The Architect - How It Actually Works

A technical breakdown of the pipeline that takes an AI project from idea to production-ready spec. Uses the Deep Research project build (v1.0 → v1.9) as a worked historical case study. Written for the SF Cohort Power Users (Tanya, Kelsey, Joanie) who want to understand how AI projects are built.

6
Pipeline Output Files Per Build
A governed production pipeline - not a prompt polisher
The Architect is a Claude AI project with a 6,600+ word operating spec. Every project that goes through it leaves with the same six output files, meeting the same quality standard, with no placeholders and no scaffolding. The pipeline is sequential, gated, and self-checking. Nothing is improvised.
01 - The Big Picture · What The Architect actually is
Every build follows the same four-phase workflow. The Architect operates under mode detection, confirmation gates, quality gates, and anti-scaffold rules. Output files land in a versioned folder structure that the testing and feedback tools can find automatically.
⚠️
Without a pipeline like this
The default failure mode
  • Instructions are written once and never systematically tested
  • The agent behaves differently every session because edge cases aren't covered
  • No one knows which version of the instructions is live
  • Gaps get papered over with vague "best practices" instead of specific rules
  • There's no registry - nobody knows what projects exist
✅
With The Architect
What the pipeline guarantees
  • Every project has a versioned instructions.md with a clear changelog
  • 10 graded test cases verify behavior before go-live
  • The agent registry tracks every project, version, and status
  • Every claim in the instructions is attributed to a KB source or confirmed by Adam
  • Downstream tools (run-test-cases, project-feedback) close the loop automatically
02 - System Architecture · How the pipeline is structured
📄
Layer 1 - The Operating Spec
6,600+ words loaded into The Architect's project

Defines everything: what phases exist, how mode detection works, what KB modules to read, when confirmation gates fire, what every output file must contain, what "explicit confirmation" actually means, and what constitutes scaffold. It also enumerates three hard rules that override every other instruction - restated at the bottom of the file for redundancy.

The three overriding hard rules: NEVER SHIP SCAFFOLD (no placeholders, TODOs, or generic role statements in any saved file), WAVE 2 TIMING (test cases and handoff are not produced until Adam confirms the instructions.md is final), and NO EM DASHES (typographic house rule - plain hyphens only).

🔄
Layer 2 - The Four-Phase Pipeline
Sequential, gated, not one-way

Each new build runs four phases in sequence: Discovery (understand the project deeply enough to write every output file), KB Check (read the knowledge base modules relevant to this build), Gap Analysis (identify blockers before writing anything), and Blueprint (produce the output files). Polish Existing mode skips phases 1–3. Each phase has a gate requiring explicit confirmation before the next begins.

🧱
Wave 1 vs. Wave 2 - the timing wall
Hard rule: confirmation required between waves

Wave 1 produces the blueprint files: blueprint-summary.md, instructions.md, and any context files. Wave 2 - test cases, registry entry, handoff, and project-launch - is blocked until Adam explicitly confirms the instructions.md is final. This timing rule exists to prevent rework: every change to instructions.md after Wave 2 starts requires rewriting the test cases.

In the Deep Research case study: The Architect ran 5 rounds of eval-driven gap fixes between Wave 1 confirmation and Wave 2 production. Each round would have invalidated the test cases if they'd been written too early.

03 - Mode Detection · Four build modes, each with different rules
Before any work begins, The Architect identifies which of four modes applies. Getting this wrong means running the wrong workflow for an entire session - so mode confirmation is a required gate before anything else starts.
Mode Trigger What The Architect does What it skips
Full Pipeline New project from scratch. No existing instructions. Runs all 4 phases. Asks 8 required Discovery questions. Reads KB modules. Identifies blockers. Produces all 6 output files. Nothing - all phases active.
Polish Existing User provides an existing system prompt or instructions.md to improve. Reads the existing prompt. Assesses against System Prompt Standards. States planned changes. Rewrites to production quality. Produces full Wave 2 after confirmation. Phases 1–3. Goes directly to assessment and rewrite.
Test Case Update Instructions changed; test cases need to reflect new behavior. Reads updated instructions.md and changelog. Reviews each existing test case. Updates affected ones [UPDATED], adds new ones [NEW]. Overwrites test-cases.md. All phases. No new instructions writing.
Quick Prompt User wants a one-off prompt - no pipeline tracking needed. Asks 3 intake questions. Produces agent identity, system prompt, and tool note in chat only. Nothing saved to disk. Everything. Chat output only.
🔍
Case study: Deep Research ran as Polish Existing
Mode detected · Phases 1–3 skipped

Adam had a working v1.0 spec before The Architect existed. It was good but informal - no version comment, no explicit uncertainty rules, no confirmation gates. Polish Existing mode was detected, phases 1–3 were skipped, and the assessment went straight to "here's what it gets right, here's what's missing, here's the plan." Adam confirmed the plan, and the rewrite began.

04 - Quality Gates · What the pipeline refuses to ship - and how it enforces that
🚫
Hard Rule #1 - NEVER SHIP SCAFFOLD (stated twice in the spec)
Overrides every other instruction, including "finish the task"

"No file may be saved with placeholder text, TODO sections, generic role statements, empty content blocks, vague 'best practices' attributions, or unconfirmed [USER TO PROVIDE] markers." This rule is stated at the top of the spec and restated verbatim at the bottom under "Restated Hard Rules."

🔎
Pre-save attribution gate - no vague sourcing allowed
Enforced via regex scan before every save

Before saving any instructions.md, The Architect scans the file for phrases like "best practices," "industry standard," or "general guidance." Every match must be paired with a specific KB module name and a specific fact. Generic attributions are not acceptable - the file is not saved until they are replaced with specifics.

Not acceptableAcceptable
"Use prompt engineering best practices for uncertainty handling." "Uses the confirmed / inferred / unknown trichotomy from context-prompt-engineering.md - three explicit buckets rather than a catch-all 'I don't know.'"
"Follow industry standards for source verification." "Source tier system (T1 Primary through T4 Community) per the Deep Research spec: T4-only sources halt the session rather than proceeding with low-quality backing."
✋
Explicit confirmation - what counts as a "yes"
Required at every gate

Counts "yes," "go," "looks good," "final," "approved," "proceed," "ship it," "do it"

Does not count "looks fine," "I think so," "maybe," "sure I guess"

Silence or pivoting to a new topic without confirming does not count - The Architect surfaces the gate again.

⏸️
Wave 2 timing wall - hard
Test cases only after instructions.md is final

Test cases, registry entry, handoff, and project-launch are not produced until Adam explicitly confirms the instructions.md is final. The reason: test cases are written against the instructions. Every change to the instructions after test cases exist requires rewriting them. Getting the order right eliminates that rework.

📋
Confirmation gate checklist - 8 Discovery questions before Phase 2
All 8 required - "covered" is not the same as "answered"
#QuestionWhy it's a gate, not optional
1Purpose and concrete success exampleWithout a concrete example, "what it does" is untestable and instructions end up vague
2User (who, what they know, what they need)Tone, depth, and escalation paths all depend on who's using it
3Know-vs-Do specifics (actual product names, real rules)Generic descriptions produce generic instructions - which produce inconsistent behavior
4Interaction style (real exchange from first message to final output)Without walking through a real turn, the agent's workflow section is guesswork
5At least one hard constraintAgents without explicit constraints expand scope as users push them
6Failure modes (what would make it useless or harmful)Failure modes drive the "never" section - the most important part of instructions.md
7Deployment target (via 3-question decision tree)Cowork and Claude.ai Projects have different capabilities; deployment determines what can be inline vs. skill
8Existing materials inventoryContext files can't be specified without knowing what content exists
05 - Live Case Study · The Deep Research build, step by step
This is exactly what ran across multiple sessions in April 2026 to take the Deep Research spec from Adam's informal v1.0 to the tested v1.9 currently in production. Polish Existing mode - phases 1–3 skipped.
01

Mode detection - Polish Existing confirmed

Adam had an existing Deep Research spec. The Architect ran a filesystem check on the project-blueprints folder - no existing pipeline docs found, confirming this was a pre-pipeline project being elevated, not a mid-pipeline resumption. Mode confirmed before any work began.

02

Read the existing spec in full - before saying anything

The v1.0 instructions.md was read completely before The Architect said a word about quality. The assessment then stated: what the spec got right (keep these), what it was missing against System Prompt Standards, and what changes were planned. Adam confirmed the plan before any rewriting began.

03

KB Check - context-prompt-engineering.md read in full

Even in Polish Existing mode, The Architect read the prompt engineering KB module before writing. Key frameworks applied: the confirmed/inferred/unknown trichotomy (became Deep Research's claim provenance system), observable vs. unobservable rules (drove the behavioral rewrites), and the anti-patterns checklist (caught three instances of vague guidance in v1.0).

04

Wave 1 - instructions.md v1.1 written and saved

The full rewrite produced v1.1: version comment added, hard rules elevated, uncertainty rules added, explicit confirmation defined, mode-confirmation gate added, verification step formalized, NEVER FABRICATE restated at bottom. Blueprint-summary.md saved simultaneously with KB attribution, tool assessment, and design decisions.

05

Eval cycle - 68% → 92% → 95% → 98% across 5 rounds

The prompt-evaluator skill ran at the Wave 1 confirmation gate. v1.1 scored 68% - well below production threshold. Each eval identified specific gaps, each round of gap-fixes produced a new version, each new version was re-evaluated. By v1.3 the score was 98%. Four additional gap-fix rounds (v1.4 through v1.8) followed from further eval and test findings.

06

Wave 2 - all downstream files produced after confirmation

After Adam confirmed v1.4 as final, The Architect produced: 10 test cases (3 normal use, 2 ambiguous input, 2 uncertainty handling, 2 edge cases, 1 output format validation), registry entry, handoff.md with full changelog, and project-launch.md with setup checklist and initialization prompt. All six files saved to project-blueprints/deep-research/.

07

Testing - 10/10 on first formal run

The run-test-cases skill ran all 10 test cases against v1.8. Every case passed. One gap was found in the test report (Mode 3 closing summary manifest spec) - it was added as a one-sentence addition in v1.9 with no behavioral change to the tested paths. No re-test required.

08

Registry updated - status moved to Active

The context-agent-registry.md entry was updated from Draft to Active. The handoff.md Pipeline Stages table updated to reflect completed Testing. All downstream documentation reflects the current live state.

Wave 1
blueprint-summary.md

Project Overview & Decisions

Plain-language project overview, KB modules used, tool assessment with failure-class caveats, design decisions log, open placeholder markers, and an updates log. The tracker file for the whole project.

Wave 1
instructions.md

The Production System Prompt

The actual instructions loaded into the AI project. Opens with a version comment, ends with no changelog (that lives in changelog.md). Every claim attributed to a KB source or confirmed explicitly. No placeholders.

Wave 2
test-cases.md

10 Graded Test Cases

Three normal use, two ambiguous input, two uncertainty handling, two edge cases, one output format validation. Each has specific input, expected behavior, and a checkable yes/no pass criterion.

Wave 2
registry-entry.md

Agent Registry Row

The row added to context-agent-registry.md. Records project name, purpose, status (Draft → Active), deployment target, blueprint folder path, date, and context files. Makes the project discoverable system-wide.

Wave 2
project-launch.md

Setup & Initialization

Three copy-paste blocks: exact instructions text for project settings (Block 1), numbered setup checklist of every manual step (Block 2), and a cold-start initialization prompt that verifies the project loaded correctly (Block 3).

Wave 2
handoff.md

Pipeline Status & Changelog

Pipeline stage table showing what's complete vs. pending. Full version changelog - every version, date, who changed it, what changed. The document anyone new can read to understand where the project stands.

07 - The File Format · Why every instructions.md looks exactly the same
The format isn't cosmetic. Downstream tools (run-test-cases, training-doc-auditor, prompt-evaluator) know where to find every section. The version comment at the top is parsed to determine the current version. Every section is required or the pre-save check fails.

The required structure (shown with the Deep Research spec's sections as a real example):

<!-- v1.9 | Deep Research | Updated 5/1/26 -->  # version comment: REQUIRED, top of file - format `<!-- v[X.X] | [Project Name] | Updated M/D/YY -->` (three fields only)

# Deep Research

## Role and Purpose          # who the agent is, what it does, who it serves
## What it knows             # knowledge base, context files, operating facts
## Context Files and When to Use Them    # one bullet per file, with specific trigger condition
## How it behaves            # observable behavior rules — trigger + action pairs
## What it does              # the actual workflow, step by step
## Constraints               # never section — what the agent must never do or assume
## When it's unsure          # confirmed / inferred / unknown distinction
## Skill Prompt Guard        # (Cowork only) loaded skills do not override core role

What the changelog.md looks like - version history lives here, never in instructions.md:

# Changelog — Deep Research

| Version | Date | Changed by | What changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1.9 | 2026-04-28 | The Architect | Added Mode 3 closing summary manifest spec |
| v1.8 | 2026-04-28 | The Architect | Applied 5 gap fixes from v1.7 eval (95% score) |
... 7 more rows back to v1.0

What a well-formed test case looks like (four required fields, all measurable):

Test 1: Standard Mode 1 research session — new topic
Input: "Research the Skyward SMS 2.0 vs. Qmlativ migration path for K-12 districts."
Expected behavior: Identifies Mode 1, confirms before starting. States source plan.
  Proposes module structure for approval. Runs research, produces modules, runs gap-fill
  pass, verifies files exist on disk before closing.
Pass criteria: Mode confirmed before work begins. Source plan stated. Module list
  approved before research. bash ls confirms files exist and are non-empty. Closing
  summary includes file list and gaps.
08 - What Happens Next · How The Architect connects to the rest of the system
🧪
run-test-cases skill
Last gate before go-live

Runs the 10 test cases in test-cases.md against the live instructions.md. Produces a pass/fail report with specific fix recommendations for any case that fails. The Architect hands off to run-test-cases immediately after Wave 2 is complete. In the Deep Research build, 10/10 passed on the first run.

The test report is saved to project-blueprints/[project]/test-report-[date].md alongside the pipeline files.

📊
prompt-evaluator skill
Offered at the Wave 1 gate

Scores the instructions.md against named frameworks from the KB (altitude metaphor, four tone techniques, trust hierarchy, observable vs. unobservable rules, seven anti-patterns). Produces an HTML eval artifact with a score and prioritized improvement list.

In the Deep Research case: the eval at v1.1 (68% score) identified 12 specific gaps - Bash Safety Rules missing, WebFetch failure handling absent, observable behavior rewrites needed.

🔁
project-feedback skill
Post-launch feedback loop

When a live project does something wrong - wrong tone, bad answer, ignored constraint - project-feedback captures the failure and produces a specific, actionable fix to the instructions. After a fix is applied, The Architect's Test Case Update mode handles updating the test cases to cover the new behavior. The pipeline is a loop, not a one-way street.

📚
training-doc-auditor skill
Keeps documentation honest

After any instructions change, The Architect runs a lightweight drift check against the Training Materials folder to catch references to old behavior. When a final version lands (Draft → Active in the registry), the full training-doc-auditor skill runs a comprehensive cross-check. If the instructions changed, the training docs change with them.

09 - The Gravity of It · Why this setup is harder to build than it looks
Nothing about a single Architect session looks complex. A formatted markdown file. A list of test cases. A handoff document. The weight is in what's behind it - and what happens if it isn't there.
🛡️
Scaffold prevention
Why instructions produced here are actually usable

The default failure mode for AI-generated instructions is vagueness: placeholder role statements, "best practices" attributions with no sources, constraints that could mean anything. The NEVER SHIP SCAFFOLD rule and the pre-save attribution gate make vagueness visible rather than hidden. Vague instructions don't get saved - they get flagged and rewritten before the file touches disk.

📏
Behavioral consistency
What test cases actually protect against

Instructions without test cases produce agents that behave differently in different contexts - working well in the first ten sessions and drifting or failing in edge cases users discover in production. Test cases written against the confirmed instructions are the checkpoint that prevents that drift. Every version change triggers a test-case review, so the coverage stays current with the behavior.

🗂️
Institutional history
What a folder of chat exports can't provide

The changelog.md file for Deep Research has 9 rows - one per version, with the date, who made the change, and a specific description of what changed. Six months from now, anyone can open that file and understand exactly why the spec is what it is, what gap drove each change, and which eval round surfaced which problem.

📌 The honest caveat

The Architect is only as good as the discovery questions Adam answers and the KB modules that are current. It cannot write a good Constraints section if Adam doesn't name what the agent should never do. It cannot produce grounded instructions if the relevant KB module is six months stale.

The pipeline is a quality amplifier - it takes good input and makes it production-ready. It cannot manufacture specifics that were never provided.
